D012-D018_h001.question:
It started a little over a year ago. I’ve been flying commercial jets for decades, so I’m used to medicals and the odd scraped knuckle in the cockpit. But after an incident on a layover—I’d rather not get into all the details, it involved a pretty bad injury—I just haven’t been the same around anything medical or bloody.

Now even walking past a clinic in the airport or seeing a needle on TV makes my chest tighten. If I have to get blood drawn for my flight physical, I’ll start sweating in the waiting room, my heart’s pounding, hands shaking, and I feel like I can’t quite catch my breath. A couple of times I thought I might pass out, so I avoid looking at the equipment or the nurse’s hands. My wife says I look pale and clammy.

I don’t have any problems actually flying, but I do catch myself worrying ahead of time about the next medical exam or if someone might get hurt on board. I try to push it out of my mind, but the physical reaction feels almost automatic when anything medical comes up.
D012-D018_h001.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Anorexia Nervosa
    C. Delusional Disorder
    D. Specific Phobia
D012-D018_h001.answer: D & A. Specific Phobia & Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D012-D018_h002.question:
It started about six months ago, after this really bad accident at a venue I was working at. I don’t like talking about the details, but since then I’ve been having a lot of trouble with certain places, especially tunnels and those long, enclosed hallways in hotels and parking garages. Elevators, too. I used to run around venues all day without thinking, and now I’ll do almost anything to avoid those areas.

If I have to go through one—like for a site visit with a couple—it’s like my body just reacts on its own. My chest tightens, my heart starts pounding, my hands get sweaty, and I feel like I can’t get a full breath. Sometimes my vision kind of narrows and I just want to turn around and get out of there immediately. It happens right away, the second I see the space or step inside.

I’m still working, but I’m rearranging floor plans, sending assistants instead of going myself, or choosing venues that don’t have those features. My husband says I seem “on edge” when we’re in parking structures or driving through tunnels, and he’s right—I’m constantly bracing for something bad to happen, even though I know it doesn’t really make sense.
D012-D018_h002.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Anorexia Nervosa
    C. Delusional Disorder
    D. Specific Phobia
D012-D018_h002.answer: D & A. Specific Phobia & Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D012-D018_h003.question:
It’s a little hard to explain, but something changed for me about six, maybe seven months ago, after that robbery at the shop. Since then I’ve become really jumpy with certain things that never bothered me before.

Loud, sudden noises feel almost unbearable now. If someone drops a tray in the café next door or a motorbike backfires outside, I just… freeze. My whole body locks up; I can’t move or speak for a few seconds, I just wait for it to be over. My staff will ask, “Are you okay?” and I can’t even answer right away.

I also get this intense fear around the idea of choking. If I eat anything with bones or big pieces of meat, I feel panicky, like something might get stuck and I wouldn’t be able to breathe. Sometimes I avoid eating in front of customers because I’m afraid I’ll embarrass myself or won’t be able to react if something happens.

I know, logically, these situations are probably safe, but in the moment it feels overwhelming, like my body takes over and I’m stuck there.
D012-D018_h003.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Anorexia Nervosa
    C. Delusional Disorder
    D. Specific Phobia
D012-D018_h003.answer: D & A. Specific Phobia & Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D012-D018_h004.question:
I guess this all really started… maybe a year or so ago? It’s hard to pin down exactly. I work part-time for the census, so I’m often driving to unfamiliar neighborhoods, crossing bridges, using parking garages. Lately, certain situations just set me off in a way that feels out of proportion.

For example, if I have to drive over one of the bigger bridges to get to an address, I start getting tense long before I reach it. By the time I’m actually on the bridge, my heart is pounding, my hands get sweaty on the wheel, and I’m almost holding my breath. It’s like something slams into me all at once—this rush of terror that I can’t talk myself out of. Sometimes I have to pull over before I even get there or find a longer way around.

Elevators are becoming a problem too. If I know I’ll have to use one in an apartment building, I feel this jolt of fear the moment the doors open. My chest tightens, and I just want to escape.

I did go through something very frightening a while back—on the road—but I don’t know if this is from that or something else. I just know these reactions feel immediate and overwhelming whenever I’m in those kinds of situations now.
D012-D018_h004.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Anorexia Nervosa
    C. Delusional Disorder
    D. Specific Phobia
D012-D018_h004.answer: D & A. Specific Phobia & Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D012-D018_h005.question:
It’s been… I don’t know, maybe around a year? Hard to say exactly, but it’s gotten worse in the last several months.  

I’m a wedding photographer, so I’m used to a little chaos, but ever since that one wedding where the groom collapsed during the reception and there was blood and paramedics and needles everywhere, I haven’t been the same around anything medical. I keep replaying parts of it in my head, but not like a movie—more like flashes when I’m not expecting it.

Now, if I even think about getting blood drawn, or see someone on TV with an IV, my whole body just locks up. It’s like I freeze in place. My heart races, but at the same time I can’t make myself move or talk. My husband had a small cut on his hand the other day and I literally couldn’t go closer to help him; I just stood there, kind of stuck, until he took care of it himself.

I’ve been putting off my own checkups because I’m scared I’ll pass out or completely shut down if they need to take blood or give me a shot. It’s starting to interfere with normal stuff, and I don’t really understand why I can’t just “push through” it.
D012-D018_h005.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Anorexia Nervosa
    C. Delusional Disorder
    D. Specific Phobia
D012-D018_h005.answer: D & A. Specific Phobia & Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D012-D018_h006.question:
I work at a salon doing nails, so I see little cuts and nicks more than I’d like. For about six months now, anything to do with blood or needles really sets me off. If a client’s cuticle bleeds even a tiny bit, my chest tightens, my heart starts pounding, my hands get sweaty and shaky, and I feel like I can’t catch my breath. I usually keep going because I can’t just walk out in the middle of an appointment, but inside I’m freaking out and just counting the minutes until it’s over.

It’s not just at work. I put off going to the doctor because I’m terrified they’ll draw blood or give me a shot. The last time I had to get a vaccine, I was lightheaded and thought I might pass out. I wasn’t always this bad. A couple years ago there was this incident—someone got hurt and there was a lot of blood—and ever since then it feels like my body just overreacts whenever anything even reminds me of that kind of thing, especially in medical settings.
D012-D018_h006.options:
A. Specific Phobia
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    D. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)
D012-D018_h006.answer: A & B. Specific Phobia & Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D012-D018_h007.question:
I run a few fast-casual places, so I’m usually fine with stress, but this is different.  

About… I’m not even sure, maybe a year or so ago, I had this incident in one of my restaurants. One of the line cooks cut himself badly on the slicer. There was a lot more blood than I expected, and it felt like the whole room shrank. My heart just took off, I got really dizzy, my hands were shaking, and I thought I might pass out. Since then, anything like that sets me off instantly.

Now I go out of my way to avoid anything medical. I’ll push off blood tests, vaccinations, even taking my kids to the doctor unless my husband can handle it. If there’s a scene with blood in a movie, I look away or leave the room. At the restaurants, if someone gets a minor cut, I walk out to the parking lot and wait until it’s handled.  

I know it sounds irrational, but the fear hits me so fast and hard that I’ll do almost anything to not be around it.
D012-D018_h007.options:
A. Specific Phobia
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    D. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)
D012-D018_h007.answer: A & B. Specific Phobia & Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D012-D018_h008.question:
I’ve been really nervous around dogs for a few years now, maybe three or four. It’s gotten worse this past year. Even if I just hear barking down the street, my chest tightens and my hands get sweaty. On the bus to my clients’ houses I keep watching out the window, worrying there might be a loose dog outside the building. The thought of one being in the hallway makes me panic before I even get there.

A while back there was an incident with a neighbor’s dog. It ran at me, barking and snapping. It didn’t really bite me badly, just scared me so much I fell and bruised my hip. Since then I avoid streets where I know there are dogs. I’ll walk a long way around or skip certain jobs if I hear the family has a big dog, even if they say it’s friendly.

I know this is affecting my work and what places I’ll go. I used to visit my sister more, but she has a dog now, so I just make excuses and stay home.
D012-D018_h008.options:
A. Specific Phobia
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    D. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)
D012-D018_h008.answer: A & B. Specific Phobia & Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D012-D018_h009.question:
I work nights as a security guard at a warehouse, so I’m used to being around dogs—we’ve always had patrol dogs on site. About six months ago, something happened on one of my shifts. I’d rather not go into all the details right now, but it involved one of the dogs, and it shook me up more than I expected.

Since then, just knowing I’ll be on the side of the building where the dogs are kept makes my chest tighten. On the way to work I catch myself running through “what if” scenarios—what if one gets loose, what if I’m alone in the corridor—and I start sweating just thinking about it. If I hear them barking on the cameras, my heart jumps even when I’m still in the control room.

I can’t really avoid them because it’s part of my job, so I force myself to do the rounds anyway. When I walk past the kennels my legs feel weak, my hands shake, and I’m watching every tiny movement they make. I try to act normal in front of the other guards, but inside I’m tense the whole time and pretty drained by the end of the shift.
D012-D018_h009.options:
A. Specific Phobia
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    D. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)
D012-D018_h009.answer: A & B. Specific Phobia & Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D012-D018_h010.question:
It’s mainly about storms and heavy rain for me. I work from home a lot, and if the forecast shows a thunderstorm, my whole day kind of orbits around it. I keep checking the radar apps, rearrange user interviews, and will cancel in-person meetings if there’s even a chance of bad weather. If I’m at the office and clouds roll in, I’ll find an excuse to leave early or stay inside away from any windows.

When it does start thundering, my body just goes into overdrive. My heart races, my hands get sweaty and shaky, I feel like I can’t quite catch a full breath, and sometimes my legs feel so weak I have to sit on the bathroom floor. I avoid traveling to places that are known for storms or where it floods easily, even if it would be good for my career.

This all got worse after that trip a couple of years ago when we got caught in that really sudden storm by the lake—boats overturning, trees coming down. Since then, I just can’t handle being near open water in bad weather at all.
D012-D018_h010.options:
A. Specific Phobia
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    D. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)
D012-D018_h010.answer: A & B. Specific Phobia & Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D012-D018_h011.question:
It started maybe… I don’t know, sometime after that accident on site a couple years back. We were doing demo and a section of the wall collapsed. A nest of rats and god knows what else came pouring out around my boots while we were trying to pull a guy out from under the concrete. Ever since then, anything small that scurries or crawls just gets to me.

On site now, if someone spots a rat or a bunch of spiders in a basement, my whole body tenses. I feel my heart pounding, my palms go sweaty, and I just freeze up for a second. I’ll call one of the guys over and stand behind them, kind of half‑joking, but I’m really using them as a shield. If my wife asks me to get something from the shed and I’ve seen mice out there, I’ll make sure she comes with me or I’ll bring a big flashlight or even a shovel, just so I feel less exposed.

I can usually push through if I have someone with me, but I avoid dark corners, basements, and old buildings when I can. It’s embarrassing for someone in my line of work.
D012-D018_h011.options:
A. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Specific Phobia
    D. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
D012-D018_h011.answer: C & B. Specific Phobia & Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D012-D018_h012.question:
I work at City Hall, so I’m used to rules and planning, but this… this feels completely out of my control.

About a year, maybe a bit more, ever since that big storm when the river flooded, I’ve had this intense reaction to bad weather. If the forecast even hints at heavy rain or strong winds, I get on edge. When the sky turns dark or the wind picks up, my chest tightens, my heart races, my hands sweat. I’ll keep checking the weather app over and over at my desk instead of focusing on files.

I can’t always avoid it—sometimes I still have to drive home in it, or sit by the window at work during a downpour—and when I do, I’m just gripping the steering wheel or the armrest, trying to hide how panicked I feel. My coworkers probably just think I’m quiet, but inside I’m thinking about that night with the flooding and how powerless I felt.

My wife says I’ve changed; I’m more on guard, especially if clouds roll in at night. I know it sounds exaggerated, but in the moment it feels overwhelming and hard to shake off, even after the storm passes.
D012-D018_h012.options:
A. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Specific Phobia
    D. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
D012-D018_h012.answer: C & B. Specific Phobia & Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D012-D018_h013.question:
It’s mainly anything to do with blood or needles. I’m fine most of the time—I sit at my setup, stream, scrim, all that—but if I even see a clip of someone getting an injection on Twitter or in a show, I feel this rush, like my whole body just drops out. My hands go cold, my heart starts pounding, and I have to look away or close the tab immediately.

It got worse after that thing that happened a while back—there was a lot of blood, and it caught me totally off guard. I don’t really like talking about it, but ever since then, anything medical sets me off way more than before. I don’t pass out, but I feel like I might.

If I have to go near a clinic, I only go if a teammate or my brother comes with me. I kind of fixate on them being there, like if I focus on talking about games or just hold onto my phone, I can get through the waiting room without freaking out. On my own, I’ll cancel or just not go.
D012-D018_h013.options:
A. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Specific Phobia
    D. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
D012-D018_h013.answer: C & B. Specific Phobia & Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D012-D018_h014.question:
I guess the main thing that bothers me now is how I am with cars and roads. Ever since that highway crash a few years back—must be five or six years now—I just can’t handle certain driving situations. If my son wants to take me somewhere and we have to go over the big bridge or through that long tunnel, I tense up straight away. My hands get sweaty, my heart starts pounding, and I can’t look out the window. 

I’ll only go if someone I trust is with me, sitting right next to me. I keep my hand on my phone the whole time, like if I’m holding onto it I’ll be safer somehow. If I have to go alone, I usually just cancel or find some long way around, even if it takes twice as long. 

I don’t know if it’s just me getting old or what, but I start worrying about it days before an appointment. I picture something going wrong, the car trapping us, and I just feel…on edge until it’s over.
D012-D018_h014.options:
A. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Specific Phobia
    D. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
D012-D018_h014.answer: C & B. Specific Phobia & Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D012-D018_h015.question:
It’s mostly this thing with tunnels and long underpasses when I’m driving. I’ll be fine on regular streets and then, as soon as I see one of those low, enclosed stretches coming up, my chest gets tight and my hands start sweating on the wheel. It’s been like this for… I don’t know, maybe the past several months? I’ll take these long detours just to avoid them, even if I’m running late for my shift at the store.

When I can’t avoid it—like if I’m with coworkers going somewhere—I’ll insist someone else drives, or I’ll call my brother to stay on the phone with me the whole time. Just hearing his voice makes it feel a little more bearable. If I’m alone, sometimes I’ll turn around instead of going through.

It started after an accident I was in last year—my car got hit in a narrow underpass. I walked away okay physically, but since then, it’s like my body overreacts in those situations. I don’t have problems all the time, but when it hits, I feel on edge and just want to escape.
D012-D018_h015.options:
A. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Specific Phobia
    D. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
D012-D018_h015.answer: C & B. Specific Phobia & Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D012-D018_h016.question:
It started about six months ago, after that code blue in the elevator at work. I was in there with a patient when it stalled between floors. He crashed, and we were doing compressions in that tiny space for what felt like forever before we got out. Since then, elevators really freak me out.

On days I’m on the wards with multiple floors, I’ll actually show up early so I can take the stairs. Just seeing the elevator doors or hearing the “ding” makes my chest tighten. The night before a shift, if I know I’m assigned to a unit where I’ll probably have to use it for transports, I’m already on edge—running through scenarios in my head, imagining getting stuck again. Sometimes it’s hard to sleep because I keep thinking about it.

I still use the elevator when I have to—like with unstable patients—but the whole time I’m in there my heart is racing, I’m sweating, and I’m just staring at the floor counter, willing it to move faster. I feel stupid about it, especially as a nurse; I know it’s irrational, but I can’t seem to shake it.
D012-D018_h016.options:
A. Binge-Eating Disorder
    B. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Specific Phobia
D012-D018_h016.answer: D & C. Specific Phobia & Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D012-D018_h017.question:
It started maybe… a year ago? I’m not exactly sure. I work at home mostly, sewing and doing alterations, so it was easy at first to just pretend nothing was wrong. But ever since that night with the gas explosion on our street—when the windows shook and the noise was so loud—I can’t handle loud, sudden sounds anymore. Fireworks, a truck backfiring, even the neighbor’s blender if it’s too high… my heart just jumps into my throat. I feel like my chest is pounding out of my body, I get shaky, sweaty, I can’t catch my breath, and all I can think is, “I have to get out of here.”

I go out of my way to avoid anything that might be noisy. I won’t go to markets on busy days anymore, I turn down invitations to family gatherings if I know there will be music or kids running around screaming. If I hear something loud coming, I’ll cross the street, or sometimes I just stay home and cancel jobs so I don’t have to leave. It’s embarrassing at my age, but I can’t seem to control how my body reacts.
D012-D018_h017.options:
A. Binge-Eating Disorder
    B. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Specific Phobia
D012-D018_h017.answer: D & C. Specific Phobia & Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D012-D018_h018.question:
I’ve always been a bit squeamish, but this past year it’s gotten out of hand, especially since that accident I saw a while back. I was walking by when someone got hurt badly and there was a lot of blood. Since then, anything to do with blood or needles really messes me up.

For example, I had to get some routine blood work a few months ago. As soon as I sat in the chair and saw the vials and the tourniquet, my whole body just locked up. It’s like I couldn’t move or talk properly. My heart was racing, I felt lightheaded, and I just stared at the floor, frozen, while they did it. I didn’t walk out or anything because I knew I needed the test, but I felt like I was going to pass out the whole time.

Even seeing medical stuff on TV, or hearing someone talk about injuries, makes me tense and on edge. I’m trying not to avoid doctors completely, but when I have to go, I force myself through it and feel awful before, during, and after.
D012-D018_h018.options:
A. Binge-Eating Disorder
    B. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Specific Phobia
D012-D018_h018.answer: D & C. Specific Phobia & Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D012-D018_h019.question:
It really started about six months ago. We took the kids to a friend’s place, and their dog just suddenly bolted toward us. It didn’t bite me, just jumped and barked right in my face. Since then, something’s… off.

Now any time I even see a dog—even on a leash, or hear one barking through a fence—my body just goes haywire. My heart starts pounding so hard I can feel it in my throat, my chest gets tight like I can’t get a full breath, my hands shake, and I start sweating. It feels like I have to get away right then.

I avoid walking in our neighborhood unless my husband comes with me. If I have to go out alone, I’ll cross the street, turn around, whatever I need to do not to get near a dog. When I *can’t* avoid it—like picking up the kids from a playdate—I’ll grip my phone or the stroller so hard my knuckles hurt, and I stay glued to whoever is with me. I keep telling myself it’s silly, but in the moment it feels completely out of control.
D012-D018_h019.options:
A. Binge-Eating Disorder
    B. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Specific Phobia
D012-D018_h019.answer: D & C. Specific Phobia & Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D012-D018_h020.question:
It started a few months ago, after something that happened at the restaurant. I’d rather not go into all the details right now, but it shook me up. Since then, I’ve developed this intense fear around loud, sudden noises in the kitchen — like when someone drops a tray or a pan slams down, or even when the blender kicks on unexpectedly.

It’s not just being startled. The second it happens, my chest tightens, my heart races, I feel like I can’t get enough air, and I have to grab the edge of a counter or my husband’s arm just to steady myself. Sometimes my hands shake so much I have to step into the office and shut the door. I can’t think straight in that moment; it’s like my body just goes into overdrive.

I’ve started organizing things so I’m up front with the customers more, as long as my husband or one of my managers is nearby. If I have to go into the kitchen during busy hours, I’ll only do it if someone I trust walks in with me and stays close. When I’m alone back there, I feel exposed, like something bad is about to happen again.
D012-D018_h020.options:
A. Binge-Eating Disorder
    B. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Specific Phobia

D012-D018_h021.question:
It started a few months ago, after that incident on the highway. I was driving back from a late-night broadcast and there was this huge pile‑up in the tunnel. I wasn’t badly hurt, but I was stuck there for what felt like forever, sirens, people shouting, nowhere to go. Since then, I can’t seem to handle certain situations.

I can still do my job on camera just fine, but anything that feels enclosed or like there’s no easy escape really sets me off. Tunnels, underground parking garages, even certain long stretches of bridge on my commute – my chest tightens, my palms get sweaty, and I feel like I’m bracing for something awful to happen again. I don’t completely avoid them because I have to get to work, but I’ll white‑knuckle the steering wheel, blast the radio to distract myself, and almost hold my breath until I’m through.

It’s embarrassing; I’m supposed to look composed for a living, but I feel ridiculous dreading a simple drive. It hasn’t stopped me from functioning, but it makes everyday routines feel a lot more stressful than they used to.
D012-D018_h021.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D012-D018_h022.question:
I’ve been preparing for the civil service exams for a few years now, so I study late, often till midnight. For about the last year or so, I’ve noticed I get unusually tense whenever there’s a heavy storm, especially at night. It’s not just discomfort; my heart races, I feel my whole body tighten, and I can’t focus on my books at all. If the lights flicker or the wind gets loud, I just sit there, rigid, waiting for it to pass.

I still stay in my room and try to continue what I’m doing because I don’t really have anywhere else to go, but inside I’m really on edge, kind of bracing myself. I keep checking the windows, imagining something going wrong, even though nothing actually happens.

A few years back, there was an incident during a bad storm—nothing I want to go into detail about—but since then, these reactions have been stronger. It’s not all the time, only when the weather turns rough, but on those days it really affects my concentration and I feel drained afterward.
D012-D018_h022.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
D012-D018_h022.answer: B & D. Specific Phobia & Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D012-D018_h023.question:
It’s mostly when anything medical is involved. I’m fine reading journal articles or seeing diagrams, but real blood or needles… I just shut down. The last time I went to the campus clinic for a routine blood test, my heart was pounding so hard I thought they’d stop the draw. My vision started to narrow, I got really lightheaded, and I had to lie down. I honestly thought I might pass out. 

I won’t go to appointments alone anymore. I make my roommate come with me and sit right next to me, or I clutch this little stone my sister gave me and don’t let go until it’s over. If I can’t get someone to come with me, I’ll usually cancel. I’ve put off vaccines and basic checkups because of this.

Part of it started after something that happened a couple of years ago in an ER with a lot of blood involved. I don’t really like talking about it. I just know that anything that even reminds me of that—like someone getting a shot in a movie—makes me tense up and I’ll look away or leave the room. It’s been like this for at least a year, maybe longer, and it feels like it’s getting in the way of taking care of my health.
D012-D018_h023.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
D012-D018_h023.answer: B & D. Specific Phobia & Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D012-D018_h024.question:
I work with flowers all day, so I’m used to sharp tools and the occasional cut, but over the last few months something’s changed with anything medical. Even just thinking about getting blood drawn makes my stomach flip. If I see blood—mine or someone else’s—I get lightheaded, my heart races, and I feel like I might pass out. I’ll look away and grab my phone or my husband’s hand and just focus on that until it’s over. I won’t go to appointments alone anymore; if my husband can’t come, I’ll cancel.  

This really started after what happened with my sister’s accident last year. I was at the hospital and there was so much blood and chaos. I still get flashes of that when I’m in a clinic or even when a customer talks about surgery. It’s not like I’m reliving it constantly, but certain smells or the sight of a needle bring it right back for a moment. I avoid health check‑ups unless I absolutely have to, and when I do go, I’m gripping my husband’s arm the whole time just to get through it.
D012-D018_h024.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
D012-D018_h024.answer: B & D. Specific Phobia & Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D012-D018_h025.question:
I guess the main thing that’s bothering me is how I’ve been reacting to storms the last several months…maybe close to a year. I’ve always been a little uneasy with thunder, but since that big storm we had last spring, it’s different. I was driving home from a late meeting at school, and the rain came down so hard I couldn’t see the road. There were branches flying, sirens, the whole thing felt out of control. Nothing “terrible” happened to me directly, but I can’t seem to shake how it felt.

Now, if there’s even a hint of bad weather, I rearrange everything. I’ll cancel evening events at the school, leave early, or insist my husband drive if I absolutely have to go out. If the forecast mentions severe weather, I stay home with all the blinds drawn, checking the radar over and over. I won’t walk near the lake anymore, even on calm days.

It feels excessive, especially for someone in my position who’s supposed to be calm for the staff and kids. I know it’s probably not rational, but when I think about being out in a storm, my chest tightens and I’ll do whatever I can to avoid it.
D012-D018_h025.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
D012-D018_h025.answer: B & D. Specific Phobia & Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
